howToUse.title: How to use semaninha
howToUse.intro: semaninha builds collages of what you listened to the most, using your Last.fm history. For that, you need an account there tracking what you listen to.

account.title: Create a Last.fm account
account.text: It's free. Last.fm keeps a history of everything you listen to, and that's where semaninha gets its data.

connect.title: Connect your player
connect.text: Every song you play becomes a "scrobble" on your profile. Spotify connects directly from your Last.fm settings, under Applications. For other players, use apps or browser extensions like Web Scrobbler.

listen.title: Listen to music
listen.text: Last.fm only records from the moment you connect. If your account is new, start with the "Last 7 days" period and a small grid, and go bigger as your history grows.

generate.title: Generate your collage
generate.text: On the home page, enter your Last.fm username (not your Spotify one), pick the period, grid size and type, then click Generate. Then just download the image.

notFound.question: I got "User not found"
notFound.answer: Make sure you entered your Last.fm profile name, exactly as it appears in last.fm/user/your-name.

notEnough.question: It says I don't have enough data
notEnough.answer: You haven't listened to enough different albums or artists to fill the grid in that period yet. Pick a smaller grid or a longer period.

noImage.question: Some covers came out black
noImage.answer: Last.fm has no artwork for those albums, so the tile is filled in black.

support.title: Help keep semaninha online
support.intro: semaninha is free and needs no sign-up, but keeping it online has costs: hosting, the domain and the server that talks to Last.fm. If the site ever made a collage you liked, consider chipping in any amount.

scrobble.title: What is a scrobble?
scrobble.intro: A scrobble is the record Last.fm keeps every time you listen to a song. Adding up your scrobbles, Last.fm builds your listening history, your stats and the rankings of your most played artists, albums and tracks — and that history is what semaninha turns into collages.

sections.title: How a scrobble is recorded
paragraphs: When your Last.fm account is connected to a player, the player tells Last.fm about each track you listen to. The record keeps the track, artist, album and the time you listened.

Not every play counts. Under Last.fm's rule, the track has to be longer than 30 seconds and be played for half its length or for 4 minutes, whichever comes first. Skipping a song right at the start doesn't create a scrobble.

sections.title: What you can do with your scrobbles
items: See how many times you played each artist, album and track, in any period.
Follow how your taste changes over months and years.
Compare your taste with your friends' on Last.fm.
Make collages and year-in-review images, like semaninha's collages and Wrapped.

sections.title: Your history starts when you connect
paragraphs: Last.fm doesn't import what you listened to before connecting your player. So on a new account, the shorter periods — like the last 7 days — are the first to have enough data for a collage. Over time, the longer periods fill up.

sections.title: Scrobbles and privacy
paragraphs: By default, a Last.fm profile's scrobble history is public, which is how semaninha can read it with just your username and no password. If you don't want a session recorded, use your player's features — on Spotify, for example, private sessions aren't sent to Last.fm.

connectPlayer.title: How to connect your player to Last.fm
connectPlayer.intro: For semaninha to build your collages, Last.fm needs to know what you listen to. That happens once you connect your music player to your Last.fm account. Here is how to do it on the most common services.

sections.title: Spotify
paragraphs: Spotify has an official Last.fm integration, and you connect it from the Last.fm website:
items: Sign in at last.fm and open Settings.
Go to the Applications tab and find Spotify Scrobbling.
Click Connect and allow access on the Spotify screen.

sections.title: After connecting Spotify
paragraphs: The integration works through your account, not the device: what you play on your phone, computer or speakers connected to Spotify gets recorded. Tracks usually show up on your Last.fm profile a few minutes after they play. Spotify private sessions aren't recorded.

sections.title: Other services and players
items: Look for "Last.fm" or "scrobble" in your app's settings: some services offer the connection right in your account.
Players in the browser, like YouTube Music, SoundCloud and Bandcamp: the Web Scrobbler extension, for Chrome and Firefox, records what plays on those sites.
On Android, apps like Pano Scrobbler record what other music players are playing on your phone.
Apple Music has no built-in Last.fm integration; you'll need a third-party app to scrobble it.

sections.title: My music doesn't show up on Last.fm
items: Check that the connection is active under Settings → Applications on the Last.fm website.
Remember that very short tracks or tracks skipped at the start don't count as scrobbles.
On semaninha, enter your Last.fm username, not your Spotify one.
semaninha only sees what is already on your Last.fm profile: if a track isn't there, it won't be in the collage either.

about.title: About semaninha
about.intro: semaninha is a free website that turns your Last.fm history into images: collages of the albums and artists you listened to the most and, at the end of the year, a year-in-review in story format.

sections.title: What the site does
items: Collages of your most played albums or artists, in grids from 2x2 to 10x10 and in a 2x6 layout.
Periods from the last 7 days to your whole history.
Wrapped, a year-in-review with your numbers, artist of the year and favorite tracks and albums.
All in Portuguese and English, with no sign-up.

sections.title: How it works under the hood
paragraphs: The data comes from Last.fm's public API, queried with the username you enter — no password is ever asked for. Artist photos come from Spotify. The image is built in your own browser, and the site doesn't store your history on any server. The details are in the Privacy Policy.

sections.title: Who makes it
paragraphs: semaninha is created and maintained by Daniel Ângelo, a developer and Last.fm user. The code is open source on GitHub, where you can also suggest ideas and report problems.

sections.title: How the site keeps running
paragraphs: Keeping the site online costs hosting and a domain. Those are covered by ads and by contributions from people who use it — if semaninha ever made a collage you liked, the Support page shows how to help.
